verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You carry a mind that feels stormy and stubborn, hard to steady like the wind. Krishna hears Arjuna say exactly this: the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful, and as difficult to hold as air. Your overthinking today is not a private failure; it is a real force that even the Gita names honestly, opening the door to what comes next.
meaning: Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He says it is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna has just described a yogi who feels the same joy and pain in all beings as in himself. Arjuna objects that such steadiness cannot last because the mind refuses to stay still. The verse proposes that the mind is difficult to steady, but practice and letting go can train it. Your overthinking is not a private flaw. It is the force Arjuna names, and it opens the way to the practice that follows.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

reading: You feel uneasy about whether you measure up while caring for your parents. Manu tells Vishnu that even before the wishing tree, he hesitates to ask for what he truly wants, doubting its power. Today, this speaks to the quiet fear that you are not good enough to name your own deepest wish. You might simply let that hesitation sit beside you, and ask for what you really want anyway.
meaning: King Manu speaks to Lord Vishnu after years of austerity. Vishnu has appeared and tells him to ask any boon. Manu feels his heart fill with doubt. He compares himself to a poor man who stands before a wishing tree yet still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing how powerful the tree truly is. He admits that one great longing remains, but he shrinks from naming it because he feels too small. You are caring for your parents and feel uneasy about whether you measure up. Manu shows that hesitation can come from not trusting how generous the giver is, rather than from any lack in you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You are carrying a feeling of loneliness while working and raising kids. Krishna tells Arjuna that one who sees him everywhere and everything in him is never lost to him, and he is never lost to Krishna. This can speak to you today as a reminder that you do not have to carry the sense of being alone by yourself; presence can meet you in the midst of your daily routines.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna while teaching him how to meditate and what a settled mind looks like. Arjuna has been asking about the nature of the self and how to hold attention. Krishna says that whoever sees him everywhere and sees everything resting in him will never be lost to him, and he will never be lost to that person. It means that when attention is widened to include the divine presence in all things and all things within that presence, separation ends.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Rama describes his restless mind to the sages.
verse_text.line: The mind pounces on a task like a bird on food, then drops it like a bored child's toy.
verse_text.translation: The mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy.

reading: You feel stuck trying to begin. Rama tells the sages that the mind swoops onto a task like a bird onto meat, then a moment later loses interest like a child with a toy. This restless pattern is an ordinary feature of the untrained mind, not a personal defect. When you sit down to study, you might notice the same swooping and dropping without blaming yourself for it.
meaning: Rama speaks to the sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha after they ask why he has grown so withdrawn. He describes his restless mind. It swoops onto a task like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy. He is naming the problem honestly. He is asking what the point of all this is, not giving the final answer. You are studying and feel stuck at the start. The verse names that restless swooping without calling it your fault.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You feel caught in overthinking while working and caring for your family. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, and that holding it feels like holding the wind. This verse names that struggle plainly, and it points to the wind itself as the image you can return to when your thoughts race today.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the highest yogi who feels all beings' joy and pain as his own. Arjuna objects that such evenness cannot last because the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. The verse names this difficulty plainly and sets up the answer that comes next. Your mind is doing exactly what Arjuna describes while you work and care for your parents and children. The verse names this restlessness without blaming you for it.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You feel restless while studying. Bali says the same day and night return, and the same tasks repeat, which to a thinking person feels like a mockery. This verse meets that weariness by naming the loop you are caught in, without judging your effort. Let the thought sit with you today as you open your books: day again, night again, the same chain of tasks.
meaning: Bali, a king who has ruled the three worlds for ages, sits by his window and wonders what his life adds up to. He sees that day follows night and the same tasks return without end. He tells himself that to a thinking person this endless round feels like a mockery. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the work is not to do more of it but to master the mind that runs it. You are studying and the same hours keep turning without giving you rest. Bali names that loop so you can see it is the repetition itself, not your effort, that is wearing you down.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You feel empty while studying, working, and caring for your parents. The Yoga Vasishtha records Rama’s attendants saying he no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work; he just keeps silent. That quiet withdrawal can be noticed and named without judgment, and letting someone else see it and stay with you is part of the story too.
meaning: A servant of Rama tells King Dasharatha that the prince has changed since his pilgrimage. He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just keeps silent. The text treats this quiet withdrawal as a real shift that calls for care and conversation, not scolding. You are carrying this same quiet across your studying, your work, and your time with your parents.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You feel empty. Young Rama asks what kingship or pleasure mean to him, and wonders who he is and what all this is for. The text treats this questioning as a healthy start, not a flaw to fix. Let his words sit with you today: if nothing feels real, you can simply ask whose it is, without forcing an answer.
meaning: Young Rama returns from his travels and sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask why he looks so low. Rama replies that he no longer sees the point of rule or delight. He asks who he really is and what all this is for. He adds that if the world is unreal, let it be unreal, and questions who truly owns anything or gains anything from it. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not as a final answer. You are caring for your parents while working, and the weight of it has left you feeling empty. Rama's question meets that exact hollow without rushing to fill it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel anxious while studying. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go, and do not last. You can bear this discomfort as something with a beginning and an end, without letting panic take over.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield just after telling him that the self moves through childhood, youth and old age. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna says that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings begin and end on their own. They do not last. Arjuna must bear them patiently without letting either joy or grief carry him away. Your anxious study sessions are part of that same flow. The tightness you feel now has a shape that changes, and it does not define the whole of you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You feel peaceful right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that the one whose happiness, delight, and light are all within becomes one with Brahman and reaches lasting freedom. That inner gladness can stay steady even while you run your own work and raise your kids. Notice the quiet source inside you today.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He describes the wise person who sees clearly. This person keeps happiness, delight and light inside. Their pleasure does not depend on what happens around them. Krishna says such a yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman while still living. You are running your own work and raising your children, and right now you feel peaceful. That steadiness already has roots inside you rather than in any single event.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You carry a sense of hope as you move through your working life. Lakshmana tells Ram that enthusiasm is powerful and that for the one who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. That same energy can show up for you today as a small, concrete step forward rather than a grand plan.
meaning: At Lake Pampa in spring, Rama is drowning in grief after Sita has been taken. Every bird and paired deer around the water deepens his longing. Lakshmana steps in and tells him that enthusiasm is powerful and that there is no strength greater than it. For the person who carries it, nothing in the world is out of reach. The verse proposes that resolute energy is the root of all effort, and by it alone the brothers will recover Sita. Your hope at work can be the same energy Lakshmana names. It does not erase what you carry, but it can carry you through the next step.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You are studying and feel angry right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born, and from attachment comes desire, which blocked turns into anger. This verse speaks to you today by tracing anger back to the mind dwelling on something it has come to want. You might notice where your thoughts keep settling, and let that observation be enough for now.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna what a person of steady mind looks like in speech and conduct. Krishna answers that such a person is content within and unshaken by sorrow. He then traces how a person who dwells on objects develops attachment. From that attachment desire is born, and when desire is blocked it turns into anger and ruin. Your anger has a starting point upstream in your attention. It helps to see where your mind keeps settling before the feeling flares.

verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You feel caught in a restless, stormy mind that refuses to settle. Krishna hears Arjuna say the mind is stubborn and strong, as hard to hold as the wind. You do not have to force it still today; simply notice where it rushes, and let that honest naming be enough.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He has just heard that a steady person sees joy and pain as the same. He objects that this is impossible. The mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. It feels as hard to hold as the wind. The verse takes this complaint seriously. It names the difficulty plainly before offering the way forward through practice and letting go. Your mind is doing exactly what Arjuna describes. It is not a failure on your part. It is simply restless, and naming that is the first honest step.

verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.

verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You feel empty right now. In the Yoga Vasishtha, young Rama asks in his father's court, "What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this?" His questioning shows that when nothing you own or do feels meaningful, it can open a real inquiry into who you are. You might sit with that question today, letting it be the start of something new rather than a problem to fix.

He asks what kingship means to him and what pleasures are worth. He asks who he really is and what all this is for. He says if it is unreal, let it be unreal, and asks whose it is and what anyone has gained. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not as a final answer. Your emptiness is not a flaw. It is the start of a real question about who you are when the usual things do not land.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You feel grateful right now. Bhartrihari wonders at his own life: the freedom to move as he wishes, food eaten without humiliation, good company, and learning that brings only calm, asking what generous austerity ripened into such a quiet mind. This plain, self-respecting life you are living—raising your kids, caring for your parents, running your own thing—can meet your eyes with the same wonder. Notice one ordinary dignity today, like a meal eaten in peace or an hour you chose for yourself, and let it simply be there.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines as a poet who has turned away from palaces and wealth. He addresses the reader who might wonder what path leads to a quiet life. He lists the goods of a simple existence. He names the freedom to wander, food eaten without humiliation, noble company, and learning that brings only calm. He adds that his mind stirs only gently even when he looks outward. He then asks what generous austerity could have ripened into such a life. In plain modern words, he treats this plain, self-respecting existence as a rare blessing. You are living a life of plain dignity right now. The verse invites you to meet your own raising of children, your care for your parents, and your own work with the same wonder Bhartrihari feels.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: You feel inspired right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one people follow. As you work and grow, your actions quietly shape how those around you handle success and pressure. Let your own conduct be the steady example you want to see reflected back.

A respected person sets the standard, and the world follows whatever that person actually does, not merely what that person says. You are building something at work and you feel the lift of that momentum. This verse holds that your own conduct is already teaching those around you how to handle success.

verse_text.speaker: Savitri
verse_text.setting: Knowing her husband will die in three days, Savitri takes a hard three-night vow; her father-in-law worries.
verse_text.line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verse_text.translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.

reading: You carry a resolve that keeps you going through study and work. Savitri tells her father-in-law that she began this hard vow with determination, and that same determination will carry her to the end. Let that steady resolve be the thing that sees you through today, right to the finish line you have set.
meaning: Savitri speaks to Dyumatsena, her blind father-in-law and exiled king. She knows her husband Satyavan will die in three days. She has begun a severe three-night vow without food. Dyumatsena is distressed by its harshness. Savitri tells him she started this with determination, and that same determination will carry it to the end. Steady love and clear speech can face even death. Determination carries what fear would drop. You began your current resolve with clear intent. That same steady force can carry you through the study and work that lie ahead today.

verse_text.line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verse_text.translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.

reading: You feel determined to keep a resolve. Savitri tells her worried father-in-law that her hard vow was begun with determination, and that same determination will carry it to the end. Your steady resolve is what started this path, and it can remain what sees it through today.
meaning: Savitri speaks to her father-in-law Dyumatsena, the blind exiled king. She knows her husband Satyavan will die in three days, so she begins a severe three-night vow without food. Dyumatsena worries at the harshness. Savitri tells him not to grieve. She says she started this vow with determination, and that same determination is what will carry it to the end. You began this resolve with clear determination, and that same steadiness can remain what sees it through today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: You feel inspired right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one people follow. As you study and move through this phase, your conduct quietly shapes how those around you approach their own efforts. Let your actions reflect the steadiness you wish to see.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just told Arjuna to act for the good of the world. Now Krishna explains why even those who have no personal need still work. A great person sets a standard by what they do. Others follow that example rather than any instruction. The wise act for the sake of the world because people imitate their conduct. As you move through your studies, the way you handle pressure and treat people becomes a quiet template for those around you.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You feel your mind is stormy and hard to steady while raising kids. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. Naming this struggle honestly is the real starting point, not a sign of failure. When the mind races tonight, simply notice it as wind you do not have to catch.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the highest yogi who treats joy and pain as his own. Arjuna objects that such steadiness cannot last. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and as hard to hold as the wind. The verse takes this complaint seriously. It proposes that the mind is difficult to steady, yet practice and letting go can train it. You are naming a mind that will not settle while you raise your children. Arjuna gives honest voice to this same restlessness, and the text treats that naming as the start of work, not a collapse.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel anxious now. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and these pass away. You can notice this discomfort as something that begins and ends, without letting it sweep you into panic. When the next wave of heat or cold arrives in your body, simply bear it patiently, as the verse says.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield after Arjuna has laid down his weapons in grief. Arjuna fears for his kin and the cost of war. Krishna begins to teach him that the self inside never dies and never is born. Then Krishna turns to the body and its experiences. He says that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These touch us and then they leave. They do not stay. Therefore Arjuna must bear them without being carried away by either joy or grief. The anxiety you carry now arises from the senses meeting a world that has shifted since retirement. It is a passing contact, not the whole of who you are.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You feel peaceful right now. Krishna says the one whose happiness, delight and light are all within becomes one with Brahman and reaches lasting freedom. You might notice that your own steadiness already carries a glow from inside, not from outside tasks or roles. Let that inner light be enough as you study, work and care for your parents today.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He is describing the person who sees clearly. This person is happy within, at ease within, and lit from within. Their joy does not come from things that begin and end. It comes from inside. That yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman while still living. You carry a quiet steadiness right now. It already comes from inside you, not only from finishing tasks or caring for your parents.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: You feel hurt right now. In the Ayodhya Kanda, Rama says the one sorrow burning his heart is that the king did not tell him himself about Bharata's coronation. The deepest pain for him was not the news, but that the person he loved avoided facing him directly. Today, you might hold the same ache: the wound lives in the silence around how it reached you.
meaning: In the Ayodhya Kanda of the Valmiki Ramayana, Rama has just learned from Kaikeyi that he must spend fourteen years in the forest and that Bharata will be crowned instead. He accepts the decree without anger. Yet one sorrow still burns in his heart. He tells Kaikeyi that the pain is not the news itself, but that his father the king did not come to him and tell him this directly. The hurt you carry now may come less from what happened and more from how it reached you. Someone close let the news travel without facing you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship him: those in distress, those seeking knowledge, those in need, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among those welcome at this door. The verse simply counts you as good exactly as you are, without asking you to fix or justify anything first.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He tells Arjuna that all four kinds worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. It does not ask them to arrive with a pure motive first. You are studying, working, caring for your parents, and raising kids. Your curiosity is one of the four doors. The verse counts you as good exactly as you are right now.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You feel hopeful as you run your own thing and raise your kids. Lakshman tells Ram that there is no strength greater than enthusiasm, and for the one who has it, nothing is out of reach. That same energy of will can meet you today in a small, concrete next step you take for your work or your family.
meaning: At Lake Pampa in spring, Rama is overwhelmed by grief after Sita is taken. Every bird and paired deer reminds him of her. Lakshmana speaks to him and says that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. The verse proposes that resolute energy is the root of all effort, and by it alone the brothers will recover Sita. You carry hope while running your own work and raising your children. That same energy of will can meet you today in a small next step for your business or your family.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: You carry a hurt that still burns. Krishna says his heart is churned like a fire-stick, and the harsh words his own relatives speak keep burning him day after day. When words from those close to us sting like this, the pain is real and it lingers. You might hold onto one harsh word today, letting it heat up again.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing tired of feuds within his own clan. He tells Narada that he gives his relatives half of what he owns, yet their harsh words still grind his heart like someone churning a fire-stick to make flame. The verse proposes that in family conflict, the only effective weapon is not force but gentleness, patience and respect. Your hurt has a name. It is the same ache Krishna carried when people he knew turned sharp with their words.

reading: Krishna describes someone whose happiness, pleasure and light are all inside: antaḥ-sukhaḥ, antar-ārāmaḥ, antar-jyotiḥ. Good days still come from outside. This joy doesn't depend on them.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: Krishna starts earlier than the outburst. Dhyāyato viṣayān puṃsaḥ: when you keep dwelling on something, you get attached, attachment turns into wanting, and wanting that meets a wall turns into anger. By the time you snap, the fire has been building for a while.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: The narrator Sanjaya speaks these words. He describes the greatest archer of his time putting down his bow and sitting in the chariot, his mind sunk in sorrow. The Gita begins with someone who can't go on, and it stays with him for seventeen more chapters.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You carry a grateful heart while studying and caring for your parents. The poet marvels at freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, good company, and learning that brings only calm, asking what generous austerity produced such a life. You already hold ordinary dignities—honest food, your own hours, and a quiet mind amid care—that deserve wonder rather than assumption.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks these lines to anyone who reads his verses. He has just turned from palaces toward a quiet life by the Ganga in Shiva's presence. He lists the gifts of a simple life. Freedom to move as he wishes. Food eaten without humiliation. Good company. Learning that brings only calm. A mind that stays gentle even after long looking outward. He asks what generous austerity could have produced such a life. He treats these plain goods as a rare blessing. He does not claim to have earned them by desert. You already hold ordinary dignities like honest food, your own hours, and a quiet mind amid care. They deserve wonder rather than assumption.

Krishna agrees that the mind is turbulent and stubborn, but he answers that practice and letting go can train it. Your thoughts are racing while you care for your parents. This verse names that exact restlessness as real, not a failure on your part.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya

verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You feel lost right now. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed by grief to go on. This verse names the moment of laying everything down when you cannot move forward. The story does not end there; the next verses show him asking for help and finding a way ahead.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna has just argued that killing his own kin would destroy their families and their ways of life. He says he would rather be killed unarmed. Sanjaya then reports that Arjuna drops his bow and arrows and sinks down on the seat of the chariot. His mind is overwhelmed by grief and he cannot go on.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna

reading: Your mind feels restless and hard to steady right now. In the Gita, Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is stormy, stubborn and as hard to hold as the wind. That honesty names what you are facing today, and it points toward the practice that follows.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes a steady mind that feels all beings joy and pain as its own. Arjuna objects that such evenness cannot last. The mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. It is as hard to hold as the wind. The Gita takes this complaint seriously and answers that practice and letting go can train it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Krishna calls these mātrā-sparśa: contacts, things that touch you and move on. A deadline, a bad week, a hard meeting. They hurt while they last, they pass, and Krishna asks you to bear them (titikṣasva) until they do.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You feel empty even while running your own thing and raising kids. Young Rama asks what kingship and pleasure mean to him, and who he really is beneath all that. When nothing you own or do feels meaningful, that emptiness can open a real question about what matters to you. You might sit with that question today, simply noticing what remains when the usual roles fall away.
meaning: Young Rama has just returned from his travels. He sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask why he seems so low. Rama answers that nothing interests him anymore. He asks what kingship and pleasure mean to him. He asks who he really is, and what all this is for. He wonders if it is all unreal, and if so, whose it is and what anyone has gained. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not as a final answer.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You carry a sense of gratitude into this season of life. The poet wonders what generous austerity has ripened into this freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, noble company, and a mind that stirs only gently. Today, this can meet you as a quiet recognition of the plain, self-respecting life you already hold.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines near the end of his Worship of Shiva. He has just reflected that moonlight, poetry and good company lose their charm once the mind sees how fleeting they are. The wise leave palaces for the forest. Now he lists the goods of a simple, even ascetic, life.

reading: You feel restless while studying. The Yoga Vasishtha has Bali say that day again, night again, the same chain of tasks mocks a thinking person. meaning: Bali, a king who has ruled the three worlds for ages, sits by his window and wonders what his life adds up to. He sees the same cycle of day and night, the same tasks returning without end. He tells himself that to a thinking person, this endless repetition feels like a mockery. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the work is not to add more of it but to master the mind that runs it. Bali's loop looks a lot like your study days right now. The restlessness you feel is the same mockery he names, and it points toward the mind behind the routine, not the routine itself.

meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after Arjuna grieves the coming war. Arjuna fears that if the self never dies, then all this pain is senseless. Krishna answers that the senses meet the world and feel cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings begin and end. They do not last. So Arjuna must bear them without being swept away by joy or grief. Your anxiousness while studying is one of those passing feelings. It is not the whole of you, and it will move on. You can sit with it without letting it carry you away.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You feel peaceful right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that the one who is happy within, at ease within, and lit from within finds lasting freedom. That inner light and quiet gladness can stay with you through your studies, simply as your own steady ground.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield as he describes the wise person who has realised Brahman. He tells Arjuna that the one whose happiness, delight and light all come from within becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman. This means pleasures that begin and end cannot hold a person's happiness. The wise find their joy inside themselves instead. You feel peaceful right now. That quiet gladness already lives inside you. It can stay with you through your studies as your own steady ground.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: You carry a hurt that outlasts the loss itself. Ram says the deepest sorrow burning his heart is not the exile, but that the one he loved did not face him to tell it directly. When someone close wounds you, the wound can include the silence around how the news reached you. You might hold that unspoken moment gently, letting it sit beside the rest.
meaning: On the morning of his coronation, Rama learns from Kaikeyi that he must spend fourteen years in the forest and that Bharata will be crowned instead. He accepts the decree without anger. Yet one sorrow burns in his heart. The king did not tell him this himself. The verse shows that a person can bear bad news. What wounds is the absence of the one who should have faced them directly and spoken the truth. Your hurt carries the weight of how the news reached you, not only the loss itself.

verse_text.speaker: Savitri
verse_text.setting: Knowing her husband will die in three days, Savitri takes a hard three-night vow; her father-in-law worries.
verse_text.line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verse_text.translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.

reading: You feel inspired to keep a resolve. Savitri tells her father-in-law that she began her vow with determination, and that same determination will carry her to the end. That steady resolve can carry your own commitment forward today, right from where you stand.
meaning: Savitri speaks to her blind father-in-law, the exiled king Dyumatsena. She knows her husband Satyavan will die in three days. She has begun a severe three-night vow, standing without food. Dyumatsena worries at its harshness. Savitri tells him not to grieve. She says she started this with determination, and that same determination will carry her to the end. Steady love and clear speech can face even death. Determination carries what fear would drop. That same steady resolve can carry your own commitment forward today, right from where you stand.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman

verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You feel hopeful about what lies ahead. Lakshmana tells Ram that enthusiasm is powerful, and for the one who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. This means that your own energy of will can carry you into new beginnings, even when the path ahead still feels wide. Let that resolve show up in one small step you take today.
meaning: At Lake Pampa in spring, Rama sits overwhelmed by grief after Sita has been taken. Every bird and mated deer reminds him of her, and his sorrow deepens. Lakshmana, his younger brother, answers this long lament by telling him that enthusiasm is powerful and that there is no strength greater than it. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach, because every kind of effort is rooted in that resolute energy. Your hope for what lies ahead already carries this same energy. It can carry you into a new beginning even while the path ahead still feels wide.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You carry a heavy sense of guilt. In this verse, Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their own will, as if pushed by some force. The Gita treats that struggle as a real question, not proof of wickedness. It invites you to simply notice the pattern you describe, without letting it define you.
meaning: Arjuna, the warrior, asks Krishna, his guide, why a person does wrong even when they do not want to, as if pushed by force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger. This anger clouds a person's wisdom and becomes the true enemy. Seeing this clearly is the first step toward mastering it. You feel guilty about past mistakes that seemed to happen against your own will. The verse invites you to name the pattern without letting it become your whole story.
